extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and advanced students of poetry and poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for evaluating and producing poetic diction and poetic works — guidance on word choice, style, metre, originality, and the balance of feeling and intellect drawn from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason for every word and position
rubrics_metrics.description: In the truly great poets... there is a reason assignable, not only for every word, but for the position of every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select each word deliberately; word-order matters. Coleridge recounts his schoolmaster's practice of examining why a sentence could not be placed elsewhere; lack of a satisfying answer indicated a fault. Anti-pattern: slovenly or arbitrary word choice/placement that could be altered without affecting meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hackneyed phrases and similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprobation of overused phrases (e.g., 'Lute, harp, and lyre, Muse, Muses, and inspirations, Pegasus...'), and banishment of repetitive similes such as the Alexander and Clytus example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on stock phrases, traditional poetic ornaments, or recurring anecdotes that fit 'too many subjects.' Coleridge gives a list of interdicted expressions and examples (Alexander and Clytus, manchineel fruit) as anti-patterns; editors should remove these clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and natural diction (manly simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for an 'austerer and more natural style' and the 'manly simplicity' re-introduced by certain poets; natural thoughts with natural diction are praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune double epithets, extravagant ornament, and turgid diction. Coleridge reports pruning his youthful 'double epithets' and taming 'swell and glitter' of diction. Anti-patterns: florid, inflated language that obscures thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction must resist paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever lines can be translated into other words of the same language, without diminution of their significance, either in sense or association, or in any worthy feeling, are so far vicious in their diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A test of good poetic language is that it cannot be recast into plain prose without loss. If a line survives unchanged in paraphrase, its diction is suspect. Anti-pattern: 'prose thoughts' dressed in poetic ornament—poetry that collapses into paraphrasable prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring power measured by rereadability
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return, with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power, and claims the name of essential poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems by whether readers return to them repeatedly with pleasure. Short-term novelty or cleverness that fades on re-reading is not essential poetry. Scoring guidance: preference for works with sustained appeal over tricks that impress only once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal poetic logic and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry... had a logic of its own, as severe as that of science; in the truly great poets there is a reason... for the position of every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems must exhibit internal coherence and reason; metaphors, images, and structures should fit the poem's internal laws. Anti-pattern: decorative imagery or phrases unsupported by sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of heart and head (feeling and intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowper and Bowles were the first who combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the one [older poets] sacrificed the passion to subtleties of intellect; the moderns to the glare and glitter of a perpetual... imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for harmony between genuine feeling and intellectual substance; avoid reducing poetry either to cold intellectual wit (epigram) or empty dazzling imagery. Anti-patterns: poetry that prioritizes point/epigram over passion, or ornament over thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty as an end (sincerity over show)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluded from the list of worthy feelings, the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader, and the desire of exciting wonderment at his powers in the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write to astonish or display cleverness; value sincere emotional and intellectual content over tricks that merely surprise. Anti-pattern: language and forms used primarily to exhibit virtuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate diction to metre and metrical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Language of metrical composition, why and wherein essentially different from that of prose... its necessary consequences, and the conditions thereby imposed on the metrical writer in the choice of his diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction that fits the metrical requirements of the poem; metre imposes constraints that impact word choice and syntax. Anti-pattern: forcing awkward words or prose-syntax into meter without regard for natural poetic phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against translating prose thoughts into verse (school-Latin influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: This style of poetry... had been kept up by, if it did not wholly arise from, the custom of writing Latin verses... Consequently he must first prepare his thoughts, and then pick out... halves and quarters of lines, in which to embody them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid methods that produce verse by mechanically mapping pre-formed prose or Latin-style thought into poetic lines. Encourage thinking in poetic terms rather than composing prose-logic then seeking poetic wrappers. Anti-pattern: verse that reads like prose with rhyme and rhythm grafted on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural language neither bookish nor vulgar
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence of 'natural language, neither bookish, nor vulgar, neither redolent of the lamp, nor of the kennel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that is authentic and dignified without pedantry or bathos. Anti-patterns: artificially bookish diction; contrived 'simplicity' that descends into vulgarity or triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the three sins of youthful poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge mentions exposing 'risu honesto the three sins of poetry' — (1) doleful egotism and recurrence of favourite phrases (trite and licentious), (2) low creeping language and thoughts under pretence of simplicity, (3) indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young writers should avoid self-indulgent egotism/triteness, feigned low/simple language, and gratuitous swelling/ornament. Coleridge reprinted sonnets mocking these faults as examples. Use revision to excise these tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline through rigorous revision and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Master's custom: place many exercises abreast, ask why a sentence shouldn't be under another thesis; if two faults of same kind found, tear up the exercise and require a new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply strict revision: identify recurring faults, require rewriting until repeated mistakes are cured. Anti-pattern: tolerating repeated defects across works; lax editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness of metaphor and image (avoid one-size-fits-all similes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain introductions, similes, and examples were placed by name on a list of interdiction... the simile of the manchineel fruit... yielded to the example of Alexander and Clytus which was equally good and apt, whatever might be the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors and similes that are specifically apt to the subject; avoid defaulting to a small set of 'serviceable' images for all themes. Anti-pattern: a narrow stock of images applied to unrelated contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for works that 'reconcile the heart with the head'
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowper and Bowles... were the first who combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the first who reconciled the heart with the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem successfully integrates emotion and reason rather than privileging one at the expense of the other. Anti-patterns: poems that are purely intellectual exercises or purely sentimental without structure or insight.
